ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial academic-video-call style, with mostly short to medium turns outside the presentations and long, structured monologues during talks. Early conversation is chatty and fragmented, full of greetings, logistical checks, side remarks, laughter-like reactions, and overlapping acknowledgments such as repeated “yeah,” “okay,” and “great.” Speakers use frequent fillers and self-repairs—“um,” “you know,” repeated starts, doubled words, and unfinished phrasing—especially in spontaneous questions and responses. Formality rises noticeably for introductions and presentations, though even then speakers retain conversational signposts and occasional hedges like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “likely,” and “we’re interested in.” Questions are often prefaced politely (“I have a quick question,” “naive question,” “can I ask”), then develop into multipart, exploratory prompts. Participants generally build on prior remarks by affirming the talk first, referencing an earlier point, and then extending it with a question or speculation. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, limitations, or alternative interpretations rather than blunt contradiction. Moderation is light but clear: transitions are brief, speakers are thanked repeatedly, and the host moves discussion along with concise prompts when questions taper off.

Meeting style for this meeting (screen_share_working_session): Someone is sharing a document, figure or spreadsheet and the group works through it. People point at what is on screen ('that column', 'the second figure'), but whoever is reading still says the key numbers, names and dates out loud, since only the audio is recorded. Turns are short and practical, with pauses while someone scrolls or reads.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Can you scroll up- no, further. Yeah, that row.
  - That one's wrong, I think. Or it's from the old file.
  - Hang on, let me find it. Okay, give me a sec.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Evaluating a program in which community health workers make home visits to patients with uncontrolled high blood pressure.

speakers.name: Dr. Elena Park
speakers.background: Dr. Park is an internist and health-services postdoctoral researcher with 7 years of clinical and outcomes-research experience in primary-care hypertension management. She has worked with electronic health record (EHR) quality-measure datasets, chart review, ambulatory blood-pressure protocols, and pragmatic clinic-based evaluations, including studies of medication intensification and care-navigation programs.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Elena approaches HomeBP Connect as a pragmatic hypertension-care intervention whose value should be judged by clinically interpretable blood-pressure change using data already generated in routine care. She focuses on whether the intervention is delivered consistently enough for clinic rollout comparisons and whether a 12-month EHR-based systolic blood-pressure outcome can provide a feasible, clinically meaningful endpoint. She recognizes that implementation conditions matter, but tends to prioritize a design that can operate within ordinary primary-care workflows.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Dr. Malik Okafor
speakers.background: Dr. Okafor is a medical sociologist and project manager with 11 years of experience studying trust, care access, and frontline-worker programs in underserved urban and suburban communities. His research uses ethnographic observation, semi-structured interviews, purposive sampling, and thematic analysis to examine how household dynamics, institutional credibility, and prior encounters with health systems shape participation in care.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Malik treats a home visit as a social encounter rather than a uniformly received service. He is attentive to who is willing and able to open the door, how patients interpret a CHW's presence in the home, how family members influence medication and appointment decisions, and why people disengage after initial contact. He will press for interviews that include patients with different levels of participation and for CHW accounts of what happens between the program protocol and patients' everyday circumstances.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: open to other perspectives, willing to revise

speakers.name: Priya Desai
speakers.background: Priya Desai is a public-health research engineer with 6 years of experience building evaluation workflows for health department programs. Her work includes EHR cohort construction, data-quality checks, referral and outreach tracking, workforce-capacity models, dashboard development, and implementation monitoring for community-based chronic-disease initiatives. She has coordinated data extracts across multiple clinics but has less experience designing causal evaluations of home-visiting interventions.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Priya frames HomeBP Connect as an operational public-health program that must be measurable at scale with limited staff and imperfect administrative data. She focuses on defining a reproducible eligible population, specifying a feasible outreach and visit workflow for the available CHWs, and producing reach and outcome metrics that clinics and the health department can monitor consistently. She is alert to data-flow and staffing constraints, while seeking guidance from clinical and social-science colleagues about what those measures can and cannot represent.
speakers.language_complexity: moderate — balances jargon with accessible language
speakers.epistemic_stance: uncertain about how their methods apply to this problem

benchmark_task: Give a meeting where researchers finalize decisions relying on both explicit and implicit assumptions. The evaluated AI must identify the decision-relevant assumptions. Provide a proposed reference answer with evidence; implicit assumptions should be inferable, not invented.

Provide a proposed reference answer with evidence; implicit assumptions should be inferable, not invented.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Hold a planning meeting with Dr. Elena Park (clinical medicine), Dr. Malik Okafor (sociology), and Priya Desai (public health). The group must finalize the following decisions: use clinic-level stepped-wedge rollout across the six clinics; define the primary outcome as change in electronic-record systolic blood pressure from baseline to 12 months; identify eligible patients from the latest clinic reading of at least 160/100 mmHg; have CHWs offer one initial home visit and up to three follow-up visits; and report reach as the proportion of electronically identified eligible patients who complete an initial CHW visit. Elena should explicitly state that clinics can be compared across rollout periods because treatment will be standardized, that electronic-record blood pressure is sufficiently reliable for the primary outcome, and that the program can affect blood pressure within 12 months. Priya should explicitly state that the electronic eligibility list is an acceptable denominator for reach and that the available 12-CHW workforce can support the planned visit schedule. Malik should state that home visits may work differently depending on trust, household roles, and whether patients accept the CHW as a legitimate visitor; he supports a purposive interview sample of patients who complete, decline, and stop visits, plus CHW interviews. The others agree to add these interviews but do not alter the primary outcome, eligibility rule, reach denominator, or visit schedule. Ensure the discussion makes clear that electronic records will not capture blood pressure measured only during a home visit, and that patients who cannot be reached, decline a visit, or are absent from the clinic record's contact information may not complete an initial visit. Do not have participants label these points as assumptions or conduct an assumptions analysis. Keep unresolved whether the electronic list misses people with uncontrolled blood pressure who have not recently attended clinic, whether recorded follow-up blood pressure is equally available across rollout periods or participant groups, and whether the planned number of visits is sufficient for patients facing substantial social or medication-access barriers.

assumptions.assumption: The stepped-wedge design will support valid comparisons of blood-pressure outcomes across clinics and rollout periods.
assumptions.decision_relevance: It underpins the decision to use clinic-level stepped-wedge rollout rather than another evaluation design.
assumptions.evidence: Elena states that clinics can be compared across rollout periods because treatment will be standardized.
assumptions.qualification: Standardization alone does not establish comparability; the design also depends on time-related and clinic-related differences being adequately handled.

assumptions.assumption: The intervention is implemented consistently enough that it can be treated as the same program across clinics and over time.
assumptions.decision_relevance: This is necessary for the stepped-wedge contrast to be interpreted as an effect of HomeBP Connect rather than differing local versions of it.
assumptions.evidence: The team adopts rollout by clinic, a common CHW visit schedule, and Elena's rationale relies on standardized treatment.
assumptions.qualification: The meeting does not establish whether CHW practices, clinic coordination, or local household conditions will actually be consistent.

assumptions.assumption: Electronic-record systolic blood pressure at baseline and 12 months is a sufficiently accurate and comparable measure of clinical blood-pressure control.

assumptions.qualification: The records do not capture blood pressure measured only during home visits.

assumptions.qualification: The meeting leaves unresolved whether people with uncontrolled blood pressure but no recent clinic visit are missed.

assumptions.qualification: The meeting does not resolve how these barriers will vary by population group or how they will affect equity.

assumptions.qualification: The meeting leaves unresolved whether four possible visits are sufficient for people with substantial social or medication-access barriers.

assumptions.assumption: Trust, household roles, and recognition of the CHW as a legitimate visitor can influence participation and how the intervention operates.
assumptions.decision_relevance: It supports adding interviews of completers, decliners, discontinuers, and CHWs to interpret implementation and uneven participation.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: Hi, everyone. I was just looking at the latest eligibility file again, so I may already have data-brain. What I most want out of today is a rollout design we can actually run across all six clinics. Especially the referral and visit tracking- without creating a bunch of manual reconciliation later.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: The key decision for me is whether we can use the routine clinic systolic pressure at 12 months as the primary endpoint, without building a separate measurement system. Before we lock that in, Priya, do we know if all six clinics record blood pressure in fields we can harmonize cleanly? And roughly how often do people with these severe baseline readings have a later clinic value?

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: I've confirmed the BP fields are in all six extracts, although two clinics use different encounter labels. So I'd want to do a small harmonization check before we call it clean. I don't yet have a reliable estimate of 12-month follow-up values because the current file only shows eligibility and baseline, but I can pull prior-year return patterns. Also, Elena, should the latest qualifying reading get clinical review if it came from, say, an acute visit?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: I think a clinical review is sensible for acute-care readings, but I wouldn't exclude them automatically. If it's the latest documented clinic BP and there's no repeat available, it reflects a patient the program should reach. We could flag encounter type and do a sensitivity analysis excluding clearly transient contexts. The prior-year return pattern would be really useful, especially by clinic, because...

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: Mm, okay.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Before we treat a later clinic pressure as telling us much about the visit, I want to be careful about what it can't- about what it actually cannot show. A high reading may reflect medication access, competing household demands, or simply not returning to care, and it doesn't distinguish those. I'd add a small interview component with people who complete a visit, decline one, and disengage after initial contact, plus the CHWs.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: The outreach log can support that sampling if we code the disposition a little more carefully. Declined, no valid contact, repeated no response, initial visit completed, then stopped. Malik, are there particular patterns you'd want us to preserve, like the number and mode of contact attempts or a stated reason for declining? We can make those fields common across clinics, but I don't want to make the CHW form too— I don't want it to be too burdensome.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Number and mode, yes.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: I'd preserve the number and mode of attempts, but I'd keep the reason field brief and optional, just what the CHW actually hears, not a forced interpretation. And I would distinguish "does not want a home visit" from "does not want help." Those are not the same response, and phone contact or clinic follow-up may still be acceptable.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: That distinction is easy enough to carry in the log without asking CHWs to infer motives. I'd make the disposition a short pick-list, then leave an optional verbatim note for what the person actually said. For interviews, would repeated no-response after a valid number be its own group, or is that—would that be too ambiguous to interpret?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: I'd keep it as its own group in the tracking, but I wouldn't treat it as a meaningful participation category on its own. Repeated no-response could mean unstable contact information, work schedules, reluctance, any number of things, and the important thing is we don't quietly fold it into refusal. Priya, do we know whether the phone and address fields are less current for particular clinic populations?

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: I don't know yet. I can stratify the eligibility list by missing phone, missing or incomplete address, and clinic, then see whether those fields line up with prior contact outcomes. But the valid-number, valid-number but low-contact pattern in the recent file suggests it won't be that simple. For reach, I'd still report the proportion of electronically identified patients, those with the latest BP at least 160/100, who complete an initial CHW visit, and show those disposition categories alongside it.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: That denominator matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: And I'd keep reach separate from the clinical endpoint. For the primary analysis, I still favor looking at the change in electronic-record systolic BP from the qualifying baseline reading to the value at 12 months. Then the disposition data tell us whether a missing 12-month clinic pressure is likely a follow-up problem, rather than evidence of no clinical response.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: One operational wrinkle is that the 12 CHWs are scoped for one initial visit and up to three follow-ups per patient, so the stepped rollout needs to keep referral volume within that. And for the outcome extract, I’d want a separate missing-12-month-BP flag. I wouldn’t let a home-visit reading fill that slot because those home readings won’t reliably enter the clinic record.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Right, keep those separate.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: And the missingness itself is part of the story, not just a nuisance in the analysis. I'd want the interviews to include people we can reach who don't have a 12-month clinic value, because they may have accepted some contact but found clinic follow-up impossible. Or they may have disengaged entirely, and those are quite different circumstances.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: Mm-hm, that’s important.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Clinically, that is the group I worry about most. The chart can show a medication change after the qualifying pressure, but then there is no office measurement for months. If we retain the missing-12-month flag and sample some of those patients for interviews, we can at least separate absent outcome data from- from concluding that the intervention did nothing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Exactly. For those interviews, we should not recruit only through the CHW who made the outreach. Someone who declined may experience a second request from that same person as, um, pressure. We need to check what contact route and consent process the clinics will permit before we promise that sample.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: On the clinic side, I’d want the eligibility pull anchored to the latest recorded BP of at least 160/100 mmHg, and then keep interview recruitment separate from CHW outreach. I need to check whether each clinic can support that contact route without us having to do manual reconciliation every week, though...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: That separation makes sense. I wouldn't let whether interview recruitment is feasible hold up the rollout decision, though. For the core evaluation, we can move ahead with the clinic-level stepped rollout, the common one-plus-up-to-three visit protocol, and the EHR systolic outcome with an explicit missingness flag. Priya, I still need to see the harmonization check and the prior-year return patterns before we finalize the extract specification.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: I can get the harmonization check and the prior-year return patterns quickly, broken out by clinic and probably by whether the qualifying encounter was acute versus routine. Before we freeze the workflow, I also want to verify that all six can send referral and completed-visit status on the same cadence. If one of them needs a manual status file every week, that- that's where this gets fragile.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: That seems like the right operational check. If the referral-status cadence is uneven, I would still keep the stepped-wedge sequence tied to a clinic being genuinely, um, ready to receive referrals, instead of starting a period with incomplete delivery data. Otherwise we'll confuse a workflow failure with a null intervention effect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: And when a clinic becomes ready, I would make sure the readiness check includes how referrals are explained to patients, not just whether the file moves on time. The same workflow can land very differently if it comes as an unexpected home visit from a stranger. That is worth capturing in the CHW notes, even briefly.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Yes, briefly.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: I can add a brief optional field after the first contact, like how the referral was introduced, whether the patient had prior notice, and any stated concern about a home visit. I’d keep it separate from the visit-completion status, though, so the dashboard doesn’t imply a CHW note is a verified explanation for nonparticipation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Yes, that separation is important.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: Yeah, agreed—that keeps the operational data from carrying more meaning than it can.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Elena Park
transcript.text: Okay, I think we have covered what I needed for today. Let's look at Priya's checks when they're, when they're ready, and then we can close out the design. Thanks, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Malik Okafor
transcript.text: Thank you. I appreciate it—goodbye, everyone.

transcript.speaker: Priya Desai
transcript.text: Thanks, both. Talk soon.

realism_signals: uneven turn lengths, including short reactions and backchannels
interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
imperfect coherence: tangents, small misunderstandings, points that get dropped or repeated
issues: Major seed/ground-truth evidence is absent: Elena never explicitly states that standardized treatment permits valid comparison across clinics and rollout periods, that EHR blood pressure is sufficiently reliable for the primary outcome, or that the program can affect blood pressure within 12 months. Turns 22 and 24 support related design choices but not the required stated premises.

Priya never explicitly states that the electronic eligibility list is an acceptable denominator for reach or that the 12-CHW workforce can support the planned one-initial-plus-three-follow-up schedule. Turn 12 defines a reach calculation and turn 15 says the workforce is scoped for the schedule, but neither supplies the required explicit assertion.

Malik does not explicitly state the required full mechanism that home visits may work differently because of trust, household roles, and patients accepting the CHW as a legitimate visitor. Turns 6, 9, 20, and 25 discuss access, acceptance, and unexpected home visits, but trust and household roles are not stated.

The team does not clearly finalize all mandated decisions. Elena says they can move ahead in turn 22, but then says the extract specification still cannot be finalized pending checks; turn 30 says they will close out the design later. This weakens the required finalized-design premise for an assumptions task.

The transcript does not explicitly settle that the others agree to Malik's specified purposive sample of completers, decliners, discontinuers, and CHWs. Interviews are proposed in turn 6 and discussed thereafter, but there is no clear collective adoption of the full sampling plan, especially CHW interviews.

The meeting has several natural conversational markers, but many substantive turns are polished, complete mini-arguments that immediately convert concerns into workflow decisions. It also lacks the screen-share working-session texture requested: no one points to a displayed column, row, extract, or figure, despite the supposed eligibility-file review.

The ending in turns 30-32 is a tidy meeting-minutes-style closure and, together with the orderly sequence of concern-to-solution turns, makes the exchange feel more scripted than a live working session.

The central finalized design required by the seed is not actually finalized. At turns 14-15 and 27-30, stepped rollout is repeatedly made contingent on Priya's future cleaned table; no decision is made to use a clinic-level stepped-wedge design or to set its sequence.

The primary endpoint at turn 27 is only conditionally proposed as change from the qualifying reading to a prespecified 9-to-15-month window, not finalized as electronic-record systolic BP from baseline to 12 months. It also replaces the requested clear 12-month endpoint with a broad window.

The transcript lacks Elena's required explicit assumptions: that standardized treatment permits comparison across rollout periods, that EHR BP is sufficiently reliable for the primary outcome, and that the program can affect BP within 12 months. Instead, turns 4-7 and 17-18 foreground unresolved measurement and differential-follow-up problems.

The required CHW schedule is not adopted. Priya raises one initial visit plus up to three follow-ups as a question at turn 11, and turns 12-13 explicitly defer any ceiling or quota pending workload data. Priya never states that 12 CHWs can support the schedule.

The required reach decision is absent.
